Question six. How do you calculate the sample size for an A B test? From four inputs: the baseline rate, the M D E, or minimum detectable effect, alpha, and power. Only the baseline comes from data. The other three are choices. Ten percent convert today, and you want to catch a two-point lift. The page's formula says three thousand eight hundred forty-three users per arm. Halve the lift to one point, and it's fourteen thousand seven hundred fifty-two, nearly four times as many. The sample grows with one over the M D E squared. A test also has to say which direction counts.

Question seven. What's the difference between a one-sided and a two-sided test? A two-sided test looks for a change either way, with two and a half percent in each tail. A one-sided test puts all five percent on the side you predicted. On the same users, power rises from eighty percent to eighty-eight. But a regression the same size, the other way, is never flagged. Features can hurt, so product tests are usually two-sided. Question eight. What is a non-inferiority test? It asks whether a new version is worse by no more than a margin set in advance. Say a cheaper checkout may cost at most half a point of conversion. At sixty thousand users per arm, the interval for the difference runs from minus point two nine to plus point three nine, clear of the margin. At six thousand, it also contains zero, but reaches past minus one. Not significant isn't the same as not worse. Then the test goes live, and someone opens the dashboard.
